title: What Every American Family Ate for Dinner in 1958

scenes.text: It's five-thirty on a weeknight in nineteen fifty-eight. In millions of American kitchens, something is bubbling on the stove and something is browning in the oven. The table is being set with the everyday dishes. A child is sent to call the others in from outside. And at six o'clock sharp, the whole family sits down together. It's time for dinner.
scenes.caption: SIX O'CLOCK SHARP

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-eight, dinner was the center of family life. Most families ate together every single night. And what they ate was remarkably similar from coast to coast. Meat, potatoes, a vegetable, bread and butter, and often a dessert. Mothers planned the menus a week at a time, and many families ate the same thing on the same night, week after week.
scenes.caption: MEAT AND POTATOES

scenes.text: So let's sit down at the table. Let's go through a typical week of dinners in nineteen fifty-eight, night by night, and see what was on the plate, what it cost, and why it tasted the way it did. If you grew up in the fifties, I'll bet you can smell some of these right now.
scenes.caption: NIGHT BY NIGHT

scenes.text: First, the shopping. Most mothers did one big trip to the supermarket each week, usually on Thursday or Friday, when the newspaper ran the grocery ads. They brought a list and a little stack of coupons. Many supermarkets gave out trading stamps, like S and H Green Stamps, which families pasted into books and traded for toasters and lamps.
scenes.caption: GREEN STAMPS

scenes.text: Let's start with the most important meal of the week. Sunday dinner. After church, the family came home to a pot roast that had been cooking slowly in the oven all morning. A chuck roast, browned in a Dutch oven, with onions, carrots and potatoes tucked around it. By the time the family walked in, the whole house smelled wonderful.
scenes.caption: THE POT ROAST

scenes.text: Sunday dinner was often eaten in the early afternoon, around one or two o'clock, and it was a big event. The good tablecloth came out. Grandparents, aunts and uncles came over. There was gravy made from the drippings, homemade rolls, and a pie or a cake for dessert. Children wore their church clothes, and were expected to behave.
scenes.caption: THE GOOD TABLECLOTH

scenes.text: Some families had roast chicken or fried chicken on Sunday instead. In the fifties, chicken was a bit of a treat. Families bought a whole bird and cut it up themselves. Mothers fried it in a cast iron skillet with lard or Crisco, and every family had its own recipe that nobody else was allowed to know.
scenes.caption: FRIED CHICKEN

scenes.text: Monday was washday, the hardest day of the week for a housewife. So Monday dinner was usually something easy. Leftovers from Sunday. The pot roast became hot roast beef sandwiches with gravy, or roast beef hash, chopped up with potatoes and onions and fried crisp in a skillet.
scenes.caption: MONDAY HASH

scenes.text: Nothing was wasted in a nineteen fifty-eight kitchen. Leftover chicken became chicken pot pie or chicken and dumplings. The bones became soup. Stale bread became bread pudding or stuffing. Bacon grease was saved in a coffee can by the stove. Mothers who had lived through the Depression and wartime rationing never threw food away.
scenes.caption: NOTHING WAS WASTED

scenes.text: Monday was also soup night in many homes. A big pot simmered on the back of the stove all day, while the wash went through the wringer. Vegetable beef soup, split pea with a ham bone, or chicken noodle. Served with crackers or a grilled cheese sandwich, it was warm, cheap and easy, exactly what a tired mother needed.
scenes.caption: SOUP NIGHT

scenes.text: Tuesday might be casserole night. The fifties were the golden age of the casserole. And the secret ingredient in many of them was a can of Campbell's cream of mushroom soup. Mixed with tuna, egg noodles and peas, and topped with crushed potato chips, it became tuna noodle casserole, one of the most famous dishes of the decade.
scenes.caption: TUNA NOODLE CASSEROLE

scenes.text: There was also the green bean casserole, invented in nineteen fifty-five by a home economist named Dorcas Reilly in the Campbell's test kitchen. Green beans, cream of mushroom soup and crispy fried onions on top. It was meant to be an easy weeknight side dish. Today, millions of families still make it every Thanksgiving.
scenes.caption: THE GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE

scenes.text: Casseroles were cheap, filling and could feed a big family with a pound of meat or a can of tuna. They were also easy to carry. When a neighbor was sick, had a new baby or lost a loved one, a casserole appeared on the doorstep, in a dish with the owner's name taped to the bottom so it could be returned.
scenes.caption: THE NEIGHBOR'S CASSEROLE

scenes.text: Wednesday might be meatloaf. Ground beef, bread crumbs or oatmeal, an egg, chopped onion, and ketchup or a can of tomato soup, all mixed by hand and baked in a loaf pan. Some mothers put strips of bacon on top, or a glaze of ketchup and brown sugar. Served with mashed potatoes and canned green beans.
scenes.caption: MEATLOAF

scenes.text: Ground beef was one of the cheapest meats in the store. In nineteen fifty-eight, a pound cost around fifty cents. Mothers stretched it as far as it could go, in meatloaf, Salisbury steak, sloppy joes, stuffed peppers, Swedish meatballs and spaghetti with meat sauce. And the leftovers made a great meatloaf sandwich for Dad's lunch the next day.
scenes.caption: STRETCHING A POUND

scenes.text: And there was liver and onions. Many children of the fifties remember it with horror. Liver was cheap and full of iron, and doctors and home economists recommended it. Mothers fried it with onions and bacon, and served it once a week or so. Kids pushed it around their plates, cut it into tiny pieces, and drank a lot of milk.
scenes.caption: LIVER AND ONIONS

scenes.text: Thursday might be the night to try something new. In the fifties, women's magazines like Good Housekeeping and Ladies' Home Journal printed new recipes every month. Betty Crocker's Picture Cook Book, first published in nineteen fifty, was in millions of kitchens. Mothers clipped recipes and filed them in a little tin recipe box.
scenes.caption: BETTY CROCKER

scenes.text: The new recipes often featured canned and packaged foods. Chicken a la king served in pastry shells. Ham slices with canned pineapple rings and maraschino cherries. Spaghetti from a can of Chef Boyardee. And for a hint of the exotic, chop suey or chow mein, made from a La Choy kit with crunchy canned noodles.
scenes.caption: CHOP SUEY FROM A CAN

scenes.text: And there was the TV dinner. Swanson had introduced its frozen turkey TV dinner in nineteen fifty-three, in an aluminum tray with three compartments. Turkey, cornbread dressing and gravy, peas and sweet potatoes. It cost about ninety-eight cents. On nights when Mom was busy, or out at a meeting, the kids got TV dinners on folding trays in front of the television.
scenes.caption: THE TV DINNER

scenes.text: And the kitchen itself was a busy place. The electric mixer whirred. The pressure cooker hissed and rattled on the stove, cooking tough meat in a fraction of the time. A radio played on the counter. And children were put to work shelling peas, peeling potatoes, setting the table and stirring the pudding.
scenes.caption: SHELLING PEAS

scenes.text: Friday was fish night in millions of homes. At the time, Catholics were not allowed to eat meat on Fridays. But even many non-Catholic families had fish on Friday, out of habit. And in schools and cafeterias across the country, Friday meant fish sticks.
scenes.caption: FISH ON FRIDAY

scenes.text: Fish sticks were a brand new invention. They were introduced by Birds Eye in nineteen fifty-three, and they became an instant hit. Breaded, frozen and ready in minutes, served with tartar sauce or ketchup. Kids who didn't like fish loved them. Other Friday favorites were salmon patties made from canned salmon, and tuna salad sandwiches.
scenes.caption: FISH STICKS

scenes.text: Friday might also be the night for macaroni and cheese, either baked from scratch with real cheddar, or from the blue box. Kraft had introduced its boxed macaroni and cheese dinner in nineteen thirty-seven, during the Depression. By the fifties, it was a staple, cheap and quick, and children have loved it ever since.
scenes.caption: MACARONI AND CHEESE

scenes.text: In the Midwest and the South, Friday might also mean a fish fry. Churches, taverns, fire halls and lodges served all-you-can-eat fried fish, with coleslaw, rye bread and potato salad, for a dollar or so. The whole family went, and it was as much a social event as a meal. In Wisconsin, the Friday fish fry is still a beloved tradition today.
scenes.caption: THE FISH FRY

scenes.text: Saturday night was often the easy night. Hamburgers or hot dogs on the new backyard grill, if the weather was good. Baked beans from a can, potato chips, and corn on the cob in summer. Or Dad might bring home a pizza, which was just becoming popular in many parts of the country outside the big cities.
scenes.caption: BURGERS ON THE GRILL

scenes.text: Some families ate breakfast for dinner on Saturday night. Pancakes, eggs and bacon. Or they went out, to a diner, a drive-in, or a family restaurant with a children's menu. In nineteen fifty-eight, going out to eat was still a treat, maybe once a month for many families. A family of five might spend five or six dollars.
scenes.caption: GOING OUT

scenes.text: Regional dinners were different, too. In New England, Saturday night meant baked beans and brown bread. In the South, it might be fried catfish, collard greens and cornbread. In Texas, chili or barbecue. In Pennsylvania, pork and sauerkraut. Immigrant families kept their own recipes alive, from pierogi to lasagna to tamales, and slowly shared them with the neighbors.
scenes.caption: REGIONAL DINNERS

scenes.text: Every dinner had sides. And in nineteen fifty-eight, many vegetables came from a can. Canned peas, canned corn, canned green beans and canned carrots, heated in a saucepan with a pat of butter. Frozen vegetables were growing more popular too. In summer, fresh vegetables came from the garden.
scenes.caption: VEGETABLES FROM A CAN

scenes.text: And then there was Jell-O. The fifties were the height of the Jell-O salad. Lime Jell-O with shredded carrots and pineapple. Cherry Jell-O with fruit cocktail suspended inside. Some even had cottage cheese, celery or olives. They were molded in fancy shapes and served on a bed of lettuce. Children either loved them or hid them in their napkins.
scenes.caption: THE JELL-O SALAD

scenes.text: Bread was white bread, usually Wonder Bread, sliced and soft, with butter or margarine. Milk came in glass bottles from the milkman, and every child drank a glass with dinner. And many families said grace before every meal, with heads bowed and hands folded.
scenes.caption: A GLASS OF MILK

scenes.text: And for dessert? Many families had something sweet every night. A slice of homemade pie. A piece of cake from a Betty Crocker or Duncan Hines mix. Rice pudding. Canned peaches. Or a bowl of ice cream, Neapolitan, with chocolate, vanilla and strawberry in one box.
scenes.caption: HOMEMADE PIE

scenes.text: Children who didn't clean their plates often didn't get dessert. Think of the starving children in Europe, or China, mothers would say, about the vegetables left on a plate. Kids argued, bargained and tried to feed their peas to the dog under the table. It almost never worked.
scenes.caption: CLEAN YOUR PLATE

scenes.text: What did all this cost? In nineteen fifty-eight, the average American family spent about a fifth of its income on food. Today, it's around one tenth. Food was a bigger share of the budget then, which is one reason mothers were so careful, so creative, and so determined to waste nothing.
scenes.caption: A FIFTH OF THE BUDGET

scenes.text: But the real meaning of dinner in nineteen fifty-eight wasn't the food. It was the table. The whole family, every night, talking about the day. Dad telling stories from work. Kids arguing about whose turn it was to do the dishes. Mom asking if anyone wanted seconds. For many people, those dinners are their warmest memories of childhood.
scenes.caption: THE TABLE

scenes.text: Today, many families eat at different times, in different rooms, in front of different screens. Maybe that's why so many people remember the dinners of the fifties so fondly. It wasn't always fancy food. But everybody was there.
scenes.caption: EVERYBODY WAS THERE

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was your favorite dinner growing up? What did your mother make on Sunday, and what dish did you hate as a kid? We read every comment, and we love the recipes. Next time, we're going to the mall in nineteen eighty-four. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR FAVORITE DINNER?
